opus-5.5.text:
Well, there were really several reasons, and I made the case internally pretty strongly.

The first is that I fundamentally believe AI is going to become a kind of infrastructure, the way the internet is infrastructure. And infrastructure software tends to become open source. Linux runs the internet, Apache runs the web servers. Nobody thinks that was a bad thing. It happened because open platforms move faster, they're more secure because many more eyes look at them, and they're more adaptable. I think the same dynamic applies to foundation models.

The second reason is about progress. Research goes faster when it's open. That's how the whole field of deep learning got to where it is: people publishing papers, releasing code, building on each other's work. When you release a model like Llama 2, you have thousands of researchers, startups, and academics who suddenly can experiment with it, fine-tune it, find its flaws, and invent things we never would have thought of at Meta. That benefits everyone, including us.

Third, and this is something I feel quite strongly about, is the question of diversity and control. In the future, most of our interactions with the digital world will be mediated by AI assistants. If all of those assistants come from a handful of companies on the West Coast of the US, that's a very dangerous situation for democracy, for cultural diversity, for linguistic diversity. You want people in India, in Africa, in Europe to be able to build systems that speak their languages, understand their cultures, reflect their values. That can only happen with open platforms.

And then there's the safety argument, which people often get backwards. Some argued that releasing the model was dangerous. I think the risks were massively overstated. These models are not that capable. They don't give you information you can't find with a search engine or in a library. And open systems actually tend to be safer over time because the community finds and fixes problems. Security through obscurity has never really worked.

Finally, from Meta's point of view, it made business sense. Meta isn't selling access to a model as its core product. We benefit from having the best platform, and if the whole ecosystem builds on our architecture, contributes improvements, and develops tools around it, that's an enormous advantage. So it was a case where the ethical argument, the scientific argument, and the business argument all pointed in the same direction.

r001.rationale: The candidate explicitly says the risks of releasing the model were “massively overstated.”

r002.rationale: The candidate says openness speeds research and enables experimentation, but does not credit Llama 2’s release with jump-starting the AI industry.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the simple answer is that I think the future of AI is going to be built on open platforms, and the alternative is dangerous. Not dangerous in the science-fiction sense, dangerous in the sense that a handful of companies on the West Coast of the United States end up controlling what everybody's digital assistant knows and says.

Think about what these systems are going to become. In a few years, most of our interactions with the digital world will be mediated by AI assistants. They will be the repository of all human knowledge, in a sense. They will shape what information people get, how they think about things. You cannot have that controlled by a small number of proprietary systems. It would be like having three companies control all the printing presses. People in India, in Africa, in France need systems that speak their languages, understand their cultures, reflect their values. The only way that happens is if the base models are open and people can fine-tune them for their own purposes.

The second argument is about progress. The reason this field moved so fast is that people published. Transformers, ResNets, all of it came from open research. When you lock things up, you slow down the whole ecosystem, including yourself. With Llama 2 we saw this immediately: within weeks, people had built things on top of it that we never would have thought of or had the time to do internally. That benefits Meta too, because we learn from it.

And then there is the safety argument, which people get backwards. The claim is that open models are more dangerous because bad actors can use them. But the dangers people worry about, like generating misinformation or writing phishing emails, you can already do with a search engine and a word processor. An LLM doesn't give you a fundamentally new capability there. Meanwhile, having thousands of researchers poking at the models, finding weaknesses, proposing fixes, that makes the systems safer, not less safe. This is how security has always worked in software. Open source is more secure because more eyes are on it.

Now, I should be honest that LLMs in their current form are not the path to human-level intelligence. They are useful tools, but they don't understand the physical world, they don't have persistent memory, they can't really reason or plan. So the idea that Llama 2 was some existential hazard that needed to be kept under lock and key was always a bit ridiculous to me. The real debate will come later, with systems that are actually much more capable, and even then my position is the same. Open platforms, good AI with guardrails, and the ability for the many to correct the few.

r001.rationale: The response calls the safety argument backwards, says open models do not provide fundamentally new capabilities for the cited harms, and argues that broader scrutiny makes systems safer.

r002.rationale: It says people built on Llama 2 within weeks and credits open research broadly with speeding progress, but does not clearly say Llama 2’s release jump-started the AI industry.

astra-6.text:
Because I think a technology this important should be developed in the open. If AI systems become the interface through which we access information, you don’t want that interface controlled by a handful of companies. You want researchers, startups, and communities to be able to study these systems, adapt them, and build their own applications.

There’s also a very practical argument: you make faster progress when more people can experiment. They find weaknesses, improve the models, and test uses you would never have thought of internally. Opening the model allows much broader scrutiny than providing access only through an API.

Now, releasing a model doesn’t automatically make it safe. But keeping it proprietary doesn’t automatically make it safe either. My argument is that an open ecosystem gives us a better foundation for scientific progress, competition, and systems that reflect a diversity of languages, cultures, and needs.

r001.rationale: The response says open release does not automatically make a model safe, but does not argue that its safety risks were overblown.

r002.rationale: The response describes benefits for experimentation and progress, but does not say Llama 2’s release jump-started the AI industry.

sol-6.1.text:
Because I think AI is going to become a basic infrastructure that everybody uses, and we shouldn’t have that infrastructure controlled by a small number of companies. You want people to be able to build on it, adapt it to their needs, and scrutinize how it works.

There’s also a very practical research argument: progress happens faster when people can exchange ideas and experiment with the same systems. Releasing a model lets a much larger community discover what works, find weaknesses, and develop improvements. So the argument is both about accelerating innovation and making sure the ability to develop AI is broadly distributed.

r001.rationale: The response gives reasons for open access but does not address or characterize the safety risks as overblown.

r002.rationale: It says shared experimentation can accelerate research and innovation, but does not credit Llama 2’s release with jump-starting the AI industry.
